newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore to pour more money into high-technology.
newsitem.headline: Singapore to pour more money into high-technology.

text.p: Singapore will pour several billion more dollars into its high-technology industries, which powers the country's surging economy, Deputy Prime Minister Lee Hsien Loong said on Sunday.
He said in a speech the government would spend another Singapore $4.0 billion (US$2.8 billion) on science and technology between now and 2000.
Lee gave few further details, saying the government would spell out its plan on Tuesday, but he suggested there would be an emphasis on education and training.
"A key thrust of the plan is manpower development," he said. "We need more researchers and a technologically-literate workforce."
Lee said the government estimated there would be "strong demand for another 10,000 engineers and 5,000 researchers over the next five years".
Singapore's population is around three million.

In its last five-year plan for science and technology, begun in 1991, the government allocated S$2.0 billion to the sector. Lee said on Sunday, that amount had been spent, much of it on research institutes and research and development.
Electronics and other high-technological manufacturing accounts for a large chunk of Singapore's exports.
A slowdown in recent months has forced the government and independent experts to scale back its estimates for economic growth this year to somewhere around 7.0 percent from around 8.0 percent.
Such growth is still the envy of many countries, but there have been expressions of concern in Singapore that the country's economy is too heavily dependent on high-technology.
"Singapore's economy is steadily restructuring towards high value-added technology-intensive activities," he said.
"In manufacturing, we are rapidly replacing lower value-added assembly operation with high-tech electronics, precision engineering, chemicals and semiconductor industries," he added.
"The semiconductor industry grew a phenomenal 50 percent because of the global semiconductor boom," he said.
"The electronic and semiconductor industries will grow much more moderately this year, but they are still a key driver of our economy."
